Central Nervous System
Physiology
Cerebellum

The cerebellum is a purely motor structure whose two halves each control the same side of the body. This lesson covers its three functional divisions, the neuronal circuits (cortex, deep nuclei, climbing and mossy fiber inputs), its roles in equilibrium, tone, and the coordination of voluntary movement, and the syndromes produced by lesions of each division.

Complete Lesson Content

General Features and Divisions

  • Cerebellar functions are purely motor.
  • Each half of the cerebellar cortex controls the motor activity of the same side of the body.
DivisionLobeMain function
ArchicerebellumFlocculonodular lobeKeeping equilibrium
PaleocerebellumAnterior lobeRegulation of muscle tone
NeocerebellumPosterior lobeRegulation of voluntary movements

Body representation

More complex than in the cerebral cortex. In the anterior lobe and the upper small part of the posterior lobe the body is represented inverted. In the larger part of the posterior lobe the representation is split into two halves, each upright.

Neuronal Circuits

  • Cortex: three layers (outer molecular, middle Purkinje cell, inner granular) containing Purkinje, granule, basket, Golgi, and stellate cells.
  • Deep nuclei: four, located in the white matter: dentate, globose, emboliform, and fastigeal. Globose and emboliform together form the nucleus interpositus.
Afferent fibersArise fromCourse and targets
Climbing fibersInferior olivary nucleusClimb around and end on Purkinje cell dendrites; collaterals excite the deep cerebellar nuclei
Mossy fibersReticular formationBranches end on granule cells, Golgi cells, and deep cerebellar nuclei

No reverberating circuits. Input-output signals are very rapid; impulses are transient and never persist for long periods.

Modification of nuclear output

  • Excitatory impulses reach deep nuclear cells from the afferent climbing and mossy fibers.
  • Inhibitory impulses reach them from the Purkinje cells.

Functions of the Cerebellum

  1. Equilibrium: function of the vestibulocerebellum (mainly the flocculonodular lobe), assisted by its connection to the labyrinth through the vestibular nuclei.
  2. Muscle tone: the paleocerebellum is inhibitory to tone; the neocerebellum is excitatory.
  3. Gross involuntary movements: via connections with the basal ganglia, motor areas, and other extrapyramidal systems.
  4. Voluntary movements (below).

Control of Voluntary Movements

Role of the spinocerebellum

  1. Motor association areas of the frontal lobe set the movement program and inform the cerebellum and basal ganglia, even before the motor area is informed.
  2. Motor area 4 excites the muscles through pyramidal and extrapyramidal tracts and informs the cerebellum of these orders via the cortico-ponto-dentato-thalamo-cortical feedback circuit.
  3. Muscle and joint performance is relayed to the cerebellum by the rapid dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts.

Servo-comparator function: the cerebellum compares (a) the program from the frontal association areas, (b) the orders from area 4, and (c) the actual muscle performance. Any error is detected and corrected immediately by:

  • Altering motor-area impulses, either braking them or enhancing contraction power, through the dentato-thalamo-cortical connection.
  • Using its wide extrapyramidal connections to raise tone in some muscles and inhibit it in others, preventing overshooting.

Damping function (preventing oscillation): movements start smoothly and end abruptly without overshooting.

  • To overcome a muscle's inertia, the cerebellum facilitates tone so contraction can begin.
  • To overcome the limb's momentum, it initiates braking impulses by stimulating antagonistic muscles, stopping the limb at the point of intention.

Ballistic movements are the most rapid, preplanned movements (e.g. finger movements in typing, saccadic eye movements in reading), set in motion to travel a specific distance and then stop. They depend on the cerebellum's biphasic function: first excitatory, then delayed inhibitory.

Role of the neocerebellum (cerebrocerebellum)

  • Programmer: the plan of sequential movements begins in sensory and premotor cortical areas and is sent to the lateral zones of the cerebellar hemispheres and the basal ganglia, which provide the plan of successive movements.
  • Predictive: anticipates the next movement while the present one occurs, making movement smooth, rapid, energy-saving, less error-prone, and purposeful.
  • Timing: times each successive movement; without it the person cannot determine when the next movement should begin.

Manifestations of Cerebellar Lesions

Archicerebellum syndrome

Flocculonodular lobe lesion causes loss of equilibrium. Characteristic drunken gait: the patient swings from side to side, walks on a wide base, and hesitates to move.

Paleocerebellum syndrome

Hypertonia; equilibrium and voluntary movements are less affected.

Neocerebellar syndrome

  • Asthenia: severe muscle weakness without paralysis, on the same side as the lesion, due to difficult initiation of contraction.
  • Hypotonia: decreased neocerebellar facilitation of the stretch reflex; the tendon jerk becomes the characteristic pendular knee jerk.
  • Cerebellar (motor) ataxia: loss of coordination of voluntary activity without paralysis.

Features of cerebellar ataxia

  1. Dysmetria: cannot adjust movement distance (hypermetria or hypometria); diagnosed by the finger-nose test.
  2. Dysdiadochokinesia: inability to perform rapid alternating antagonistic movements; the hand on the diseased side follows the intact side.
  3. Staccato speech: words are broken into letters (e.g. "Alexandria") due to tremors of speech muscles.
  4. Kinetic (intention) tremors: rhythmic oscillations during voluntary movement, especially at its end; absent at rest and in sleep. Due to loss of damping, i.e. a series of cortical corrections of overshoot followed by overshoot of the corrections.
  5. Cerebellar nystagmus: side-to-side eye movements while fixing on an object, attributed to tremors of the extraocular muscles.
  6. Rebound phenomenon: inability to stop a rapidly moving limb suddenly, from failure of braking. Tested by the arm pulling test: sudden release of resisted elbow flexion may make the hand strike the face.
  7. Decomposition of movements: complex movements are fragmented, from loss of the programmer function.
  8. Abnormal (zigzag) gait: in a unilateral lesion the weak side (hypotonia) is pushed by the strong healthy side, so the patient deviates toward the weak side; in bilateral lesions the patient swings from side to side.

Types of ataxia

TypeCause of disturbanceExample
Sensory ataxiaSensory input from the musclesTabes dorsalis, thalamic syndrome
Motor ataxiaMotor output from the cerebellum to the musclesNeocerebellar syndrome

Key Points / Quick Review

Divisions

  • Archi (flocculonodular): equilibrium
  • Paleo (anterior): tone, inhibitory
  • Neo (posterior): voluntary movement, tone, excitatory
  • Each half controls the same side

Circuits

  • Climbing fibers: inferior olive; mossy fibers: reticular formation
  • Both excite deep nuclei; Purkinje cells inhibit them
  • No reverberating circuits

Movement control

  • Servo-comparator: program vs. orders vs. performance
  • Damping: facilitation to start, braking to stop
  • Ballistic: excitatory then delayed inhibitory
  • Neocerebellum: programmer, predictive, timing

Lesions

  • Archi: drunken gait, wide base
  • Paleo: hypertonia
  • Neo: asthenia, hypotonia (pendular knee jerk), ataxia

Ataxia features

  • Dysmetria (finger-nose test), dysdiadochokinesia
  • Staccato speech, intention tremor, nystagmus
  • Rebound (arm pulling test), decomposition, zigzag gait
